description: The world no longer has a single leader. **multipolarity** is redistributing the power cards, and no one yet knows who will write the new rules.

hero.hook: For twenty years, a single country dominated the planet. This era is coming to an end.

blocks.text: For a long time, the world was dominated by a single superpower: the United States. This shift towards a world where several poles of power coexist, **multipolarity**, is one of the major turning points of the 21st century.

This change is not just about the economy. It redefines sovereignty, the strength of alliances and the way of resolving conflicts. The end of the Cold War suggested a unified world order. The reality turns out to be much more complicated.

For almost forty-five years, international relations were dominated by **bipolarity**: two rival blocs, the West led by the United States via **NATO**, and the East under the influence of the USSR. This tense balance offers a certain stability, each side avoiding direct confrontation thanks to nuclear deterrence.

The fall of the USSR in 1991 put an end to this face-to-face. The American editorialist **Krauthammer** then speaks of : for the first time since the Roman Empire, a single nation dominates all areas. The United States is becoming a hyperpower with no credible opponent. **[[“Unipolar moment” (Krauthammer)]]**
This American "unipolar moment", between 1991 and 2008, was one of the shortest empires in history, before China and Russia began to challenge American supremacy.
This period is reflected in increasing interventionism: from the Balkans to the Middle East, Washington acts as a “world policeman”, sometimes under UN mandate, more and more often alone.

sections.title: From bipolar balance to American hegemony

blocks.text: The shift towards multipolarity comes from several national trajectories which challenge Western hegemony. The main driving force is the rise of **China**, which became “the factory of the world” before transforming its economic power into military ambition. Through the , Beijing weaves an immense network of influence. **[[New Silk Road]]**

**Russia**, for its part, is making an aggressive strategic return, refusing the order born in 1991 which it considers humiliating. Other countries, such as **India**, claim strategic autonomy. Many find themselves within the , an organization which allows them to influence the G7. **[[The BRICS]]**
India illustrates this new world: it buys Russian oil despite sanctions, carries out military exercises with the United States and sits alongside China within BRICS.
Active middle powers, such as Turkey, complete this picture. The world is no longer organized around an ideology, but around a pragmatism where each actor seeks to maximize their sovereignty.

Managing global issues becomes very complicated in a multipolar world. The UN Security Council is the first witness: the massive use of the right of veto often prevents any effective resolution of major conflicts.

blocks.caption: The rise of several rival powers is reshaping the global balance inherited from the Cold War.

blocks.text: This multipolarity also creates a fragmentation of standards. Where the West defends universal values ​​linked to human rights, the new poles often advocate non-interference, which complicates the fight against climate change or the regulation of new technologies.

The global economy is also feeling this tension, with a form of selective deglobalization, “friend-shoring”, where trade is concentrated between countries sharing the same interests. Far from guaranteeing peace, multipolarity seems for the moment to create chronic instability.

For some theorists, such as the American John Mearsheimer, this multipolar world is unstable, because it encourages competition for regional hegemony and increases the risk of miscalculation between great powers. The end of the single protective umbrella forces many countries to rearm.

However, multipolarity also offers a chance to democratize international relations. For the countries of the Global South, this world opens up an unprecedented freedom of choice: no longer being a satellite, but an actor capable of negotiating with several poles at the same time.

The world order is no longer a garden tended by a single hand, but a space where several forces coexist. The stability of the 21st century will be based on the ability of all to manage divergent interests.

The American “unipolar moment” after 1991 lasted less than twenty years. China, Russia, India and other powers are now contesting the dominance of a single pole, ushering in an unprecedented period of global competition.
